Uauy and Dangour (2009) discussed the fat and fatty acid requirements and recommendations for infants aged 0–2 years and children aged 2–18 years, as published in the Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism. 2. UNICEF (2007) provided a framework for assessing infant and young child feeding practices, including definitions and conclusions from a consensus meeting held in Washington, DC, in November 2007. 3. UNICEF (2017) released a report titled The State of the World’s Children, which highlights global issues affecting child health and nutrition. 4. Vandenplas et al. (2014a) evaluated the safety of soy-based infant formulas in children, as published in the British Journal of Nutrition. In a separate study (2014b), Vandenplas and colleagues developed a Belgian consensus statement on the use of growing-up milk for children aged 12–36 months, published in the European Journal of Pediatrics. 5. Verduci et al. (2019) examined the nutritional aspects of cow’s milk substitutes for children, including milk from different mammalian species, special formulas, and plant-based beverages, as published in Nutrients. 6. Victora et al. (2008) explored the long-term consequences of maternal and child undernutrition on adult health and human capital, as part of the Maternal and Child Undernutrition Study Group, published in The Lancet. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published several guidelines and reports: In 2001, WHO released a guide for program managers on the assessment, prevention, and control of iron deficiency anemia. In 2003, WHO outlined a global strategy for infant and young child feeding. In 2005, WHO provided guiding principles for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months. In 2014, WHO issued a policy brief on global nutrition targets for 2025, focusing on wasting. In 2018, WHO clarified the classification of follow-up formulas for children aged 6–36 months as breastmilk substitutes. 8. Woldu et al. (2014) investigated the consumption of unmodified cow’s milk and its association with iron deficiency anemia in infants and toddlers, as published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences and Research. 9. The World Bank (2017) reported on the prevalence of anemia among children under five years of age. 10. Xuan et al. (2013) conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the effects of growing-up milk containing synbiotics on immune function and growth in children, published in Clinical Medicine Insights: Pediatrics. 11. Ziegler and Fomon (1983) demonstrated that lactose enhances mineral absorption in infancy, as published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition. In 2007, Ziegler reviewed the adverse effects of cow’s milk in infants, presented in the Nestlé Nutrition Workshop Series. 12. Several studies assessed the risk of bias in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies using tools such as ROBINS-I. 13. The GRADE framework was used to evaluate the quality of evidence in studies comparing animal milk, follow-on formula, low-fat milk, plant-based milk, and fortified milk for children aged 12–23 months. Evidence was often downgraded due to small sample sizes, high risk of bias, and imprecision in effect estimates. 14. Specific trials, such as those by Akkermans (2016), Sazawal, and Svahn, reported on outcomes like iron deficiency, growth, and immune function. However, many studies faced limitations, including unclear randomization methods, lack of blinding, and incomplete reporting of baseline characteristics. 15. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed based on factors such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, baseline comparability, blinding, and selective reporting. Many studies were supported by private industry but analyzed independently to minimize bias. 16. This summary provides a clear and professional overview of the content, emphasizing the key studies, methodologies, and findings related to child nutrition and milk-based interventions.
